question: Hold the description and the dog's choices still. Let each swarm build everything else from the bottom up. Do the choices survive, and is each world its own?

swarms.name: Terry Gilliam
swarms.made: The real archive dog from a 1930s home movie, cut out by its mask and engraved by hatching its own light; card parts on pins, a tail cut from its own back fur. Every other figure is a found public-domain cut-out, engraved the same way.
swarms.moved: Card pivots, held frames and hard substitution. The call turns the woman's head into a hinged shouting mouth and the dog's head into a door; the refusal is the card turned over to its blank back, stamped NO; the approach is earned by the door swapped for a lit slab; the lying is a lying card.
swarms.trick: Each choice is a substitution, so the dog's decision is also the film's cut.
swarms.dog: the real archive dog, cut out and engraved, on card pivots

swarms.name: Lotte Reiniger
swarms.made: A hand-cut shepherd silhouette of 23 pieces on 22 pins, its proportions measured from the archive dog's pose keys (not traced). Tissue hills, a card house front, black card with holes the lamp shines through, lace-cut ornament.
swarms.moved: Articulated joints on a lit screen, paws planted by a contact solver; turns are made by swapping in cut end-on pieces (a rear view, a front view) and four interchangeable heads, and the head always leads the body.
swarms.trick: No colour on any figure: the whole relationship has to read by outline and the gap between shapes.
swarms.dog: a hand-cut silhouette of 23 pieces on a lit paper screen

swarms.name: Frank Mouris
swarms.made: Thousands of tiles cut from 55 public-domain archive shots (2,238 frames), each figure a computed shape whose edge is the tiles themselves, down to 4×3 pixels, with no line drawn; the tiles' subjects mean something: the dog is animals and the archive dog, the person faces and hats, the door doors and ladders, the light lanterns and bulbs, the words alarm clocks and trumpets for COME HERE, flowers and swans for it's all right.
swarms.moved: The torrent's speed is the dog's state: frantic under the calls, every tile of the dog replaced at each choice, settling as it lies down, and still holds where each tile only plays its own shot forward.
swarms.trick: The voice is made of pictures too, and it hits the dog as a ring of alarm clocks.
swarms.dog: a torrent of tiles cut from 55 archive shots

swarms.name: Peter Foldès
swarms.dog: drawn contour keys whose points correspond, blended pose to pose
swarms.made: Contour keys drawn as coordinates: 16 body keys and 10 head keys, each stroke with a fixed point count so that point i is the same place on the dog in every key. The archive dog was studied for proportion, not traced; the person, the house, the door and the dusk are drawn the same way.
swarms.moved: In-betweens are weighted blends of corresponding points, paced to the score; turns pass through drawn rear and front views where a symmetric key swaps its correspondences. Shapes change as consequences: the caller swells and the reaching arm is drawn long; the refusing dog closes into a curl; the door's outline is carried out onto the boards as its light.
swarms.trick: The door's outline is lifted off the door and laid on the porch as the light.

swarms.name: Ivan Sutherland
swarms.made: Points, lines and arcs on a simulated phosphor vector display. The dog is a 24-point graph under 77 hard constraints (bone lengths, joint sides, floor contact, and the threshold itself), its proportions the archive dog's measured bones; nothing else is borrowed.
swarms.moved: A real iterative solver, warm-started every frame, with its residuals on the console. The prompts are light-pen drags: the reach pulls the hand toward the dog until the console says HAND GOAL UNSATISFIABLE. The dog cannot be dragged at all.
swarms.trick: THE DOG IS NOT SELECTABLE: the brief's 'understand it, not control it', said in Sketchpad's own terms.
swarms.dog: a 24-point graph under 77 constraints, solved every frame

swarms.name: South Park lineage
swarms.dog: flat construction-paper pieces, a whole drawing per view and posture
swarms.made: Biscuit: about 25 flat construction-paper pieces cut in code, each with a fixed scissor wobble so it looks the same every frame; three body views, five head views, a standing and a lying drawing, and an atlas of eyes, brows and ears. Maren, the person, has one view, stand, crouch and sit postures and a ten-drawing mouth atlas. Five Quick, Draw! doodles make the moon, trees and fence. Original designs, not the show's.
swarms.moved: Every turn or change of posture is a swap to another whole drawing, held on twos, never squashed; the head is turned separately from the body and leads it. Paws are put down and stay put; one list of timed sounds drives her mouth and her voice. The limited animation does the acting: a held sulk, eyes rolled up on the approach, one back-of-head drawing for looking in.
swarms.trick: The fewer drawings it has, the more each choice of drawing says.

swarms.name: Dynamic pose selection
swarms.made: Real people's Quick, Draw! dog doodles, chosen by eye from 4,164 and labelled by pose; the house, door, moon, steps, arm and hand are doodles too, drawn on in their makers' stroke order.
swarms.moved: A decoder picks a whole drawing for every pair of frames, with costs for pose, for changing identity and for swapping off a footfall. A drawing is only scaled, moved or mirrored, never bent.
swarms.trick: The dog that turns its back is the same drawing as the dog that comes.
swarms.dog: whole Quick, Draw! doodles by real people, chosen, never bent

swarms.name: Multiview substitution
swarms.dog: a separate drawing for each view, swapped at its own pivots
swarms.made: Separate drawings made in code for this film: three body views (profile, rear three-quarter, rear), lying versions of the rear two, and four head views, the other side by flipping a near-symmetric dog (dark saddle, pale collar ring, dark tail). The archive dog gave markings and proportions only.
swarms.moved: A turn is a swap to the next view, never a squash or a rotation: the head goes first, the body follows one view at a time, the feet step at each swap, and the torso stays on the score's x through every swap. The door is the only thing that rotates, because a door is flat.
swarms.trick: It solves the turns, the place every earlier swarm failed, by never pretending the dog is a solid.

swarms.name: Secondary dynamics
swarms.dog: spheres and capsules, with ears, tail, coat and tag on solved springs
swarms.made: A dog solved and drawn in code from spheres and capsules: six torso spheres, neck and head, muzzle, four legs, two ear flaps, a seven-node tail, a collar with a tag; proportions and coat studied by eye from the archive dog, no archive pixel in the film. The person has a scarf; the door is wood on a hinge; there is a shrub.
swarms.moved: The primary motion follows the score, with planted feet that step. Everything secondary is solved, never keyframed: ears, tail, coat, tag, scarf, shrub and the door are springs and dampers pulled toward the pose, colliding with bodies, floor and lap, and dying away in the holds. The person's one push is sized so the door reaches its stop at 6.20 s.
swarms.trick: Nothing secondary is animated by hand, so stillness has to be earned: the holds are quiet because the energy has gone.

swarms.name: Atlanta Moving Image
swarms.made: No drawing at all. The archive dog's own footage, masked frame by frame; the woman and the door from Straight Talk, the seated man from Survival Stresses, the hand from The Door to Heaven, the wall and path from the home movie. A live strip above the stage shows every source frame in use, with its title, year, rights and the operation applied.
swarms.moved: Re-timing and re-ordering recorded motion: its walk mirrored and played backward is the retreat; its own turn away from a person is the refusal; the door's closing swing run backward is the opening. The one pose the footage never recorded, lying down, is composed and marked COMPOSED on screen.
swarms.trick: The scene says what it is the whole time: COMPOSED SCENE · archive fragments re-performed · not a recorded event.
swarms.dog: the archive dog's own footage, re-timed and re-ordered

swarms.name: Provenance graph
swarms.dog: cuts from one archive frame and its own turning frames, every layer hashed
swarms.made: One frame of the home-movie dog cut along its SAM mask and recorded cut lines into head, body and legs, the tail from another frame, each in a dusk and a lamplight colouring; the dog's own turning frames for both turns. The Straight Talk door, a woman cut from Straight Talk, the hand from The Door to Heaven, a miner's lantern from Anthracite, wall stone from the home movie, Quick, Draw! moon, trees and fence. Every image is a node in a 367-node lineage graph with a content hash, its parents, its operation and its rights.
swarms.moved: Pivots and a planted-foot walk for the puppet; hard substitution through single clean archive frames for the turns; the door's closing swing played as its opening. Every frame is composed only from its recorded layers: 287 derived images re-run from source reproduce their hashes, and frames rebuilt from the records alone match the render bit for bit.
swarms.trick: The film can answer, for any pixel, where it came from and what was done to it.
